title: Universal traversal sequences under arbitrary labels
formal: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm \(A\) and absolute positive integers \(C,b\) such that, for every pair of integers \(n,d\ge1\), on input \((1^n,1^d)\) the algorithm outputs in at most \(C(n+d+2)^b\) steps a word \(w=w_1\cdots w_T\in[d]^T\), with \(T\le C(n+d+2)^b\), satisfying the following universal property? For every connected undirected \(d\)-regular port-labeled multigraph on \(n\) vertices in the convention below and every starting vertex \(s\), the walk that successively takes absolute port numbers \(w_1,\ldots,w_T\) visits all vertices.
why: A universal traversal sequence replaces all random choices in a walk by one short deterministic instruction list, without inspecting the graph. Efficient construction under arbitrary local labels would expose how far randomness can be removed when a walker cannot use information about its incoming edge or leave memory on vertices.
status_note: The construction question is explicit in Vadhan’s 2012 text. The 2025 full exploration manuscript and September 2026 journal abstract/introduction were checked for model differences; neither states a matching polynomial-time UTS construction. The May 2026 weighted-PRG report concerns a different generator guarantee and was not treated as a traversal theorem. Bounded searches through 14 September 2026 located no matching resolution. This does not exhaustively certify current openness.

sentences: A universal traversal sequence is one list of absolute local port numbers that visits every vertex of every graph of a specified size and degree.
The graph may have parallel edges and self-loops, and its local port labels are arbitrary.
The question asks for a deterministic polynomial-time constructor given only the size and degree parameters.
Short sequences are known to exist, but incoming-port-based exploration and polynomial cover time with expensive local computation are different guarantees.
An efficient construction would remove randomness from graph-independent traversal under severely restricted information.

definitions:
Use \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). A port-labeled multigraph is specified mathematically by a map \(h:[n]\times[d]\to[n]\). The \(d\) ports at each vertex are distinct local labels; different ports may lead to the same neighbor. Undirectedness means \[ \forall u,v\in[n]:\quad |\{i:h(u,i)=v\}|=|\{j:h(v,j)=u\}|.\] This represents equal directed multiplicities in opposite directions. A self-loop is allowed and consumes one port, following the textbook’s directed-edge convention. A graph is connected when any two vertices are joined by a finite walk through its ports. No compatibility between the port numbers at opposite ends of an edge is imposed.

For a word \(w\) and start \(s\), define \(v_0=s\) and \(v_t=h(v_{t-1},w_t)\) for \(1\le t\le T\). Universality requires \(\{v_0,\ldots,v_T\}=[n]\). The same word must work for all maps \(h\) obeying those conditions and for every start. At step \(t\), the word specifies the absolute outgoing port \(w_t\), independently of the vertex, prior walk, or the port through which the walker arrived. There is no incoming-port-dependent offset, backtracking instruction, mutable vertex memory, or graph-dependent change to the word.

The constructor receives only the unary size and degree parameters, not \(h\), \(s\), a graph oracle, advice or a random seed. It is one finite deterministic multitape Turing program; all its work, preprocessing and output are counted. Each port number is output in binary with a delimiter, so writing the entire sequence is included in the polynomial time bound. The polynomial is in the values \(n,d\), not their binary encoding lengths. This card selects the polynomial-time construction explicitly offered in Open Problem 3.9; a logarithmic-workspace constructor is a stronger possible outcome, not an additional requirement. The target is exactly \(n\) vertices as in Example 3.8. For a parameter pair admitting no connected graph in this convention, the universal condition is vacuous.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that a uniform constructor with the stated polynomial bounds exists, including universality for every local labeling and every starting vertex, or prove that no such constructor exists. Nonconstructive existence of a short sequence is insufficient, as is a construction whose running time is superpolynomial. A universal exploration sequence whose next outgoing port depends on the incoming port is a different object and does not by itself meet this target. The negative answer concerns all such constructors, not the failure of one proposed sequence.

context_blocks.text: The textbook uses undirected multigraphs with arbitrary local port labels. Polynomial-length words visiting every vertex of every graph in a fixed size/degree class exist, as recorded in Example 3.8. The open issue is the efficient deterministic production of such words.

Open Problem 4.48 restates Open Problem 3.9. The earlier statement expressly permits polynomial-time construction as a target and also mentions the stronger logarithmic-space possibility. This card retains the first option and the full multigraph family; the complete-graph example in the later statement is not substituted for the general target.

The textbook records polynomial-length logspace constructions for a restricted consistent labeling convention, and quasipolynomial-length constructions for general labels. A consistently labeled graph there has no two distinct vertices with the same \(i\)-th neighbor for any fixed port \(i\). Arbitrary labels in this card do not satisfy that promise.

The 2025/2026 exploration paper carefully distinguishes absolute-port traversal sequences from universal exploration sequences that can use the incoming port. It also separates the number of moves from the time spent computing them: a nonconstructively chosen traversal word can have polynomial cover time even when its local computation is extremely expensive. Its newer algorithms may keep mutable memory on vertices. These model differences prevent their cover-time guarantees from answering the construction question here.
